desc:
The string s contains lowercase letters and balanced round brackets. Process the brackets from the innermost pair outwards: for each matching pair, reverse the whole text between the two brackets (as it looks at that moment) and remove the brackets themselves.

Return the final string, which has no brackets.

Example: '(u(love)i)': the inner pair turns love into evol, giving (uevoli); reversing that gives iloveu. Another: 'a(bc)d' becomes 'acbd'.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters '(' and ')'
The brackets in s are balanced
The answer may be empty, for example for '()'
hints: Reversing every bracket group directly costs O(length of group) each time, which can add up to O(n<sup>2</sup>) for deeply nested groups. First make it correct, then fast.
A stack of partial results works: on '(' start a new buffer; on ')' reverse the buffer and append it to the buffer below.
For O(n): first record the matching partner of every bracket with a stack. Then walk through the string; whenever you hit a bracket, jump to its partner and flip the walking direction.
editorial: Simple solution: keep a stack of strings. A letter is appended to the top buffer. On '(' push an empty buffer. On ')' pop the top buffer, reverse it, and append it to the new top. This is easy to get right but can copy O(n) characters at each of O(n) nested levels.

A linear solution uses the matching pairs. Precompute pair[i] with a stack. Start at index 0 moving right. When the pointer lands on a bracket, jump to its partner and reverse the direction, then continue stepping. Letters met along the way are output in exactly the order the nested reversals would produce, because passing through a bracket mirrors you into the group's text from the other side. Every character is visited once, so time is O(n) and space is O(n).
